readerTitle: Growing with a hole in the bucket
caseNote: 가상 사례 (기장 대행 회사, 수영장 관리 업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이탈은 고정된 숫자가 아니라 비율이라서 사업이 커질수록 함께 커지고, 결국 '매달 새 고객 수 ÷ 이탈률'에서 성장이 멈춘다.
misconception: 매달 새 고객이 꾸준히 들어오면 고객 수도 꾸준히 늘어난다. 월 3~5% 이탈은 작은 숫자라 신경 쓸 필요가 없다.

sources.text: 고객 이탈률(churn rate)과 정상 상태(steady state) 고객 수의 표준 계산

factChecks.note: 상한선(ceiling) = 매달 신규 ÷ 월 이탈률. 10 ÷ 0.05 = 200, 10 ÷ 0.025 = 400. 평균 유지 기간 ≈ 1 ÷ 이탈률: 5%면 20개월, 2.5%면 40개월.

cards.title: Growing with a hole in the bucket
body: A small bookkeeping firm signs 10 new business clients every month. It never misses. The owner expects a steady climb.
Three years later, the firm is barely bigger than it was after two. Nothing went wrong with sales. The problem was a number that looked too small to worry about.

image.label: A bucket being filled while water leaks from a hole
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 수도꼭지에서 물이 일정하게 양동이로 들어가고, 양동이 옆 작은 구멍에서 물이 새어 나감. 물 높이가 중간쯤에서 멈춰 있는 느낌. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where will the firm be in three years?
body: You have 100 clients. You add 10 new ones every month. Each month, about 5% of your clients leave: they close, switch firms or do it themselves.
If nothing changes, how many clients will you have after 36 months?

options.feedback: That's the number with no one leaving. It counts every new client and ignores the ones walking out the back door.

options.text: About 280: you gain 10 and lose 5 each month
options.feedback: Good instinct to subtract losses. But 5% of 100 is 5; 5% of 180 is 9. Losses grow as you grow, so the net gain keeps shrinking.
Right. Each month you lose 5% of a bigger base, until losses equal the 10 you add. The next card shows the climb flattening.

cards.title: Same sales effort, very different curve.
body: With no churn, the firm adds 120 clients a year. With 5% monthly churn, it adds 46 in year one, 25 in year two and 13 in year three.

image.label: Same sales, churn compounds the hole
image.brief: Two growth curves: no churn vs 5% monthly churn flattening.

cards.title: Churn compounds
body: **Churn rate** is the share of customers who leave in a period. Here, 5% a month.

Because it's a percentage, it hits a bigger base every time you grow. Growth stops when the number leaving equals the number arriving. That point is your **ceiling**: new customers per month divided by churn rate.
For the firm: 10 ÷ 5% = 200 clients. Selling harder moves the ceiling. Selling the same never gets past it.

image.label: Line rising and flattening under a dotted ceiling at 200
image.brief: 단순한 선 그래프. 선이 100에서 시작해 빠르게 오르다 점점 완만해지며 점선 "Ceiling: 200"에 다가감. 옆에 "10 new ÷ 5% churn = 200" 공식 라벨.

cards.title: Small monthly gaps grow into big ones.
body: Compare two firms that differ by just 2 points of monthly churn. After two years, the gap is 19 points. Monthly churn always looks small. It's the months that stack.
cards.softwareNote: Subscription apps usually report churn monthly. A 3% monthly rate looks harmless on a dashboard, but it means losing about 30% of paying users within a year.

cards.title: Halve churn, double the ceiling.
body: If the firm cut churn from 5% to 2.5%, its ceiling would jump from 200 to **400 clients**, with the same 10 new clients a month.
Each client would also stay about twice as long on average: roughly 40 months instead of 20. That's twice the fees from every client you worked to win.
The same math runs a lawn care route, a hair salon or an IT support contract. Anything people pay for again and again has a ceiling.

cards.title: One average churn rate hides a lot.
body: Churn is rarely steady. New customers often leave faster than long-time ones, so a single average can mislead you. Splitting customers by when they joined helps, and that's the next lesson.
The ceiling also assumes new customers keep arriving at the same pace.
And not every loss hurts. Losing a client who costs more to serve than they pay can raise profit even as your count falls.

cards.title: Now it's a pool cleaning company.
body: You have 250 homeowners on weekly service. Every month, about 4% cancel, roughly 10 this month. Your ads reliably bring in 12 new customers a month.
Where are you heading if nothing changes?

options.text: Up about 144 a year, to roughly 394
options.feedback: That counts every new customer and none of the cancellations. It's the plan that leads to hiring too many cleaners.

options.text: Up 2 a month, to about 274 in a year, and climbing
options.feedback: Close for year one. But losses rise as the base grows, so the climb doesn't continue. It flattens out.
Yes: 12 ÷ 4% = 300. To grow past it, you must either win more customers each month or lose fewer. Busier crews alone won't do it.

cards.title: Churn is a percentage, so it grows with you.
body: Your new customers per month divided by your churn rate tells you where growth will stop. Small changes in churn move that ceiling a lot.
**Try it today:** divide customers lost last month by customers you had at the start of the month. Then divide your monthly new customers by that rate. That's your ceiling.
